correctness.rationale: A uniformly spherical exposing direction is equivalent to 2n independent standard Gaussian objective coefficients. All partial matchings are vertices, with rank multiplicities 1,2n,n(n-1), and row/column symmetry is orthogonal in the Frobenius metric. Rank zero requires all negative coefficients, giving 2^(-2n). For a specified rank-one vertex (row1,col1), its necessary and sufficient inequalities are x>0,y<x,Y_j<0,X_j<min(x,x-y) for every j>1; splitting y<=0 and 0<y<x reduces the probability to the stated positive Gaussian integral B_n. The remaining rank-two angle follows by partitioning the almost-sure unique maximizer. The Gaussian-maximum density n phi Phi^(n-1) and the asymptotic J(t)~1/(sqrt(2pi)t) give the 1/sqrt(pi log n) relative rare-rank correction via uniform tail control; finite n tests do not prove that limit.
risks: The mean-field numerical quadrature becomes unstable for extremely tiny exponentially rare probabilities at very large n; the analytic asymptotic avoids this.
Ambient Euclidean/Frobenius geometry is essential; projected partial permutohedra have different normal cones.

value.rationale: Two rows are the first nontrivial matching dimension with competition between choices in different rows. Complete normal-cone angles of all matching ranks are a natural geometric invariant; their exponential smallness and the explicit 1/sqrt(log n) relative correction precisely quantify how often Gaussian linear optimization chooses a deficient matching. These constants provide a reusable asymptotic benchmark beyond generic combinatorial vertex counts.
risks: Metric-specific and fixed two-row setting; not an all-rectangular family or a universal matching asymptotic.
